Causes of Economic Growth

ECON 104 · October 1, 2026

Review

  1. Economic growth is important.
  2. Economic growth is enough, and only economic growth is enough.
  3. Economic growth can be understood as a shift of the PPF (an increase in productive capacity) and a shift of the demand curve (an increase in wages). These two are not different!
  4. As people become more productive, their wages are higher!
  5. There has been tremendous economic growth in human history.
  6. Where has this come from?

Imagine you are stranded on an island

Poster: Cast Away (2000)
Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)
ECON 104
04

How do you survive?

  • You consume 5 coconuts a day.
  • Can you survive on only coconuts? No. No protein or other important nutrients.
  • You want to eat fish.
  • But you’re terrible at catching fish.
  • To catch 1 fish, you need to give up 3 coconuts.
  • So, you can either have 5 coconuts; or 2 coconuts and one fish.
  • But you want more fish.
    • What can you do?
ECON 104
05

Trade-offs. Trade-offs.

  • You take down 2 coconuts, but instead of trying to catch fish, you invest time in building a spear.
  • You spend 7 days making a spear.
  • It doesn’t work.
  • You spend 7 more days making another spear.
  • This one works!
  • Now, you can have 2 coconuts AND 3 fish.
2 coconuts + 1 fish
Before the spear
14 days
Spent making spears (7 + 7)
2 coconuts + 3 fish
After the spear
ECON 104
06

What have you done here?

  • You have increased your production.
  • With that, you have also increased your consumption.
  • But, let’s think about this in two time periods — present and future.
  • In the present, you had to reduce your consumption (we call this saving) and invested this in capital formation (the spear).
  • The spear came to fruition in the future, which allowed you to consume more in the future!
PresentConsume less (saving)
→
InvestCapital formation (the spear)
→
FutureConsume more!
ECON 104
07

How do economists think about this?

The factors of production

  1. Labor (your own efforts)
  2. Capital (the spear). But this can take many forms — physical capital, human capital, and technological knowledge.
  3. Land (the natural resources available)
  4. Organization (we’ll discuss this more)
These are more immediate causes of growth. Why is it that some countries have more capital and more productive labor than others?
ECON 104
08

Capital

  • Capital increases labor productivity!
  • When people use capital, they become more productive!
  • Someone employed on a farm is more productive when they use a tractor, versus when they use a hand plow.
  • The typical farm worker in the U.S. uses more capital than the typical worker in India. Guess who gets paid more?
ECON 104
09

Capital increases labor productivity!

Tractor with a chisel plow

Ploughing with oxen, West Bengal, India

ECON 104
10

Human Capital

  • Human capital is like making an investment in yourself!
  • Taking the time to educate yourself so that your productivity increases in the future.
  • You also improve human capital by training and on-the-job experience.
  • Why do you accept lower pay for internships? You are saving (reducing your consumption) to invest in increasing your productivity for the future!
ECON 104
11

Technological Knowledge

  • Technological knowledge is knowledge about the best (lower cost) ways to produce things!
  • Imagine 1000 shovels cost the same as a machine to dig. Would you buy the 1000 shovels or the machine?
  • The machine is better technology.

13

Back to the Island

  • What if we introduce another person on this Island?
  • And now, you both specialize and trade!
  • You’ve become much better at fishing now — thanks to your spear and the human capital you have built up from learning.
  • The other person, who’s a good forager, has figured out the best spots to get fruits and berries.
  • You can both now have fruits/berries and fish.
  • You eventually also discover fire.
ECON 104
14

You can also benefit from team production!

  • Some things are better with two people working on producing something, than them separately doing it.
  • If you had to build a boat — it would probably be more effective for both of you to build the boat together.
  • In a hospital, there is division of labor between the doctors, nurses, technicians, radiologists, etc. — but they are all coordinated by the management!
ECON 104
15

ECON 104
16

Limited by the extent of the market

  • Let’s say that building a boat and a net allows you to catch 50 fish per day!
  • That’s very productive — but you both need to give up almost all your consumption of coconuts and fish to invest towards that.
  • Would you build the boat and a net? No. The market (here two people) is not large enough for you to benefit from building a boat.
  • Let’s now introduce 10 other people on the island — if they all pay you and your (now) friend three fish and three coconuts each to build the boat to have more fish in the future — would you do it? Perhaps yes!
ECON 104
17

Adam Smith

Portrait of Adam Smith (public domain), Wikimedia Commons

“That the Division of Labour is Limited by the Extent of the Market.”

Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Chapter III
ECON 104
18

Risk from appropriation

  • If you are worried about someone stealing your spear, would you invest the effort in making the spear?
  • If you are worried that someone will take the boat and run (sail) away with it, would you build the boat?
  • NO.
  • What do you need here?
  • (Secure) property rights!
Secure means that they must be enforceable — you need punishment mechanisms for people who violate property rights.
ECON 104
19

Is government the answer?

  • You build a government (give 3 people the power to adjudicate and enforce) to protect property rights.
  • What if these 3 people themselves decide to take away your boat?
  • What can you do?
  • Secure property rights mean not only that other people don’t take it away — but also that the government (state) doesn’t take it away!

The case of the two Koreas

Henderson, Storeygard & Weil (2009), NBER; graphic by Geopolitical Futures
  • Does geography explain the divergence of the two Koreas? (or the wealth on our island)?
  • Does culture explain the divergence of the two Koreas?
ECON 104
22

Institutions

  • Before Korea was divided at the end of WWII, they shared the same people, culture, and geography.
  • Similar levels of physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technological knowledge.
  • They differ in one very important way—broadly speaking, South Korea embraced the institutions of capitalism, and North Korea had communism.

Economic and Political Institutions

What institutions incentivize economic growth and development?

  • Property rights!
  • Competitive and open markets!
  • Political stability and honest government (regime uncertainty)
ECON 104
26

The 3 P’s

1

Property Rights

2

Prices

3

Profits (and losses)

ECON 104
27

Prices

  1. Prices are signals wrapped in incentives.
  2. Prices communicate valuable information about resource scarcity and relative values through just a single number!
ECON 104
28

Profit and Loss

  1. Profits and losses tell you whether you’ve used the resources productively or not.
  2. If I use my resources in ways that others value, I am rewarded with profit.
  3. If I do not create value for others, I suffer losses.
  4. This encourages investment, innovation, and experimentation.
  5. Incentivizes hard work and risk-taking.
ECON 104
29

Economic Freedom and Prosperity

Evidence from countries around the world

ECON 104
30

Measuring Economic Freedom

Fraser Institute index: 165 jurisdictions, five areas

1

Size of Government

Government consumption; transfers and subsidies; government investment; top marginal tax rates; state ownership of assets

2

Legal System & Property Rights

Judicial independence; impartial courts; property rights; military interference; integrity of the legal system; contracts; real property; police and crime

3

Sound Money

Money growth; standard deviation of inflation; inflation in the most recent year; foreign currency bank accounts

4

Freedom to Trade Internationally

Tariffs; regulatory trade barriers; black-market exchange rates; control of the movement of capital and people

5

Regulation

Credit market regulations; labor market regulations; business regulations; freedom to compete

Source: Fraser Institute, Economic Freedom of the World: 2025 Annual Report.
